rationale: Abstract 7 describes a small-expanded TBP allele with an SCA17 movement phenotype and visual hallucinations. Abstract 32 evaluates the pharmacologic pantothenate-kinase modulator BBP-671 in healthy volunteers. Blood acetyl-CoA is measured after the drug, without testing dietary pantothenate or dried figs. These are separate participants and outcomes.

The collection separates a voriconazole safety report in patients with hematologic disease and abstract 261 on quinine toxicity during malaria treatment. The latter records auditory and visual hallucinations after co-treatment and reports subsequent clinical change. Neither series tests dried figs or counts visual episodes in Parkinson disease.

The review compares motor outcomes and adverse-event rates under monoamine oxidase-B inhibition, including visual hallucination reports with adjunctive drug use. It does not record dried fig consumption or food-timed visual episodes.

This review describes the phenomenology, potential causes and study methods for hallucinations and delusions in Alzheimer disease. Its discussed interventions and patient groups provide no dried fig comparison in Parkinson disease.

The investigators study alpha-synuclein pathology in infant Krabbe brain tissue. The dataset identifies visual hallucinations in an older Lewy body dementia donor used separately for pathological context. No participant has a measured dried fig exposure with clinical episode counts.

The systematic review compiles patient-reported visual complaints across studies and distinguishes them from functional visual tests. It documents heterogeneity in phenotyping and does not identify an intake comparison using dried figs or a defined change in visual episode frequency after food.

The review examines relationships among neuropathological Lewy body findings, clinical diagnoses and symptoms such as hallucinations. The underlying results concern disease classification instead of dried fig intake or food-linked clinical changes.

The human-study review compares sensory processing and pharmacologic evidence and cites earlier uncontrolled ondansetron reports in Parkinson hallucinosis. It identifies the ongoing TOP HAT trial as separate. Neither medicine nor the reviews establish a dried fig exposure or episode result after food.

The retrospective series assesses 69 immunotherapy-naive autoimmune limbic encephalitis patients and compares neuropsychological and clinical features. The patient population and outcome assessments do not track dried fig intake or Parkinson visual episode frequency.

The methods study ranks network measures for functional imaging and examines robustness across modeling choices. Its endpoints characterize network analysis without a measured culinary exposure or clinical hallucination series.

This imaging comparison measures changing brain states associated with cognitive fluctuation in Lewy body dementia. The fluctuation and imaging endpoints do not measure intake-associated visual episodes or dried fig exposure.

The original describes clinical and biomarker differences among progressive dysexecutive presentations due to Alzheimer pathology. The cognitive and behavioral observations do not test dried figs or count visual episodes in the target Parkinson population.

The review discusses neuromodulation for cognitive outcomes and cites the small active-versus-sham basal forebrain trial that reports exploratory visual symptom changes. It is not an additional sample and supplies no food exposure comparison.

The meta-analysis synthesizes resting imaging connectivity differences in Parkinson disease and other synucleinopathies. Its inclusion criteria concern patient-control imaging contrasts. It does not measure dried fig intake or a visual event trajectory.

The cohort compares tau accumulation and clinical measures in probable Lewy body dementia and cognitively unimpaired controls. Tau uptake and longitudinal cognitive measures are distinct from visual episode frequency after consuming dried figs.

The cohort compares biomarker trajectories across mild cognitive impairment with Lewy bodies and Alzheimer categories and applies the North-East Visual Hallucinations Inventory. Ratings are higher in probable Lewy body cases than in the Alzheimer-type group. The later plasma paper reuses pTau181 measurements. Neither gives a dried fig intervention or food-timed visual episodes.

The paper discusses separating acute psychedelic perceptions from later psychological treatment effects. The proposed framework concerns pharmacologic exposures and does not address frequency of visual hallucinations after dried figs in Parkinson disease.

The prospective multicenter classifier validates EEG features against two dementia diagnoses. Hallucination histories may inform diagnostic phenotyping. The analysis measures neither dietary exposure nor visual episode frequency after food.

The investigators examine genetic relationships and variation across subgroups of Lewy body dementia. Clinical hallucination status helps describe the phenotype. No recorded exposure or outcome is attributable to dried fig consumption.

The original case reports atypical parkinsonism, behavioral changes, visual hallucinations and a preference for sweets in a Huntington expansion carrier. The preference is not a measured dried fig intake, and the clinical report has no food-timed comparison.
The case examines brain tissue after a tremor-related Parkinson intervention. The procedure and tissue findings do not involve dried fig ingestion or a measured visual hallucination outcome.

The review summarizes clinical red flags, manifestations and differential diagnosis across Parkinson and other parkinsonism syndromes. Visual hallucinations serve as clinical context without an assigned food exposure or event count.

The optical coherence tomography study measures inner retinal layers and diagnostic performance in Parkinson participants and controls. Visual hallucinations appear as context for visual dysfunction, without a food intervention or visual symptom comparison following intake.

The review compares diverse device therapies and motor responses in genetic Parkinson series. A cited case reports intermittent visual hallucinations in a device-treatment setting. No included dried fig exposure or food-timed episode count was identified.

Researchers compare serotonergic and noradrenergic findings in 24 Lewy body disease donors with clinical histories emphasizing depression or delusions. This tissue analysis does not measure an oral fig contrast or count visual episodes.

FDG PET data compare 79 DLB, 63 Alzheimer disease and 41 control participants. Metabolic network measures concern diagnosis and disease topography, with no intake exposure or meal-associated visual event tracking.

The review describes locating symptom-related circuits and includes visual hallucination findings from prior lesion studies. A mapped visual network is neither an administered dried fig exposure nor a prospective clinical episode endpoint.

The review describes approved and investigational pharmacologic treatments for Parkinson motor symptoms. Medication trials may report visual hallucinations as adverse events. No ordinary dried fig exposure or food-linked episode count is provided.

The paper reviews skin findings that can help recognize movement disorders. The reviewed cutaneous and neurological associations do not establish a dried fig intervention or visual episode frequency in Parkinson disease.

The study compares performance among 22 DLB, 22 Parkinson and 22 age-matched control participants. Visual task accuracy and threshold are perceptual measures, not spontaneous visual episodes. No dried fig intake is assigned or measured.

The panel proposes patient-caregiver screening and clinician follow-up for hallucinations and delusions. It discusses patient reporting, diagnostic and therapy context. The clinical recommendations provide no original dried fig or episode-frequency comparison.

Five of six participants from the earlier basal forebrain stimulation trial enter long-term follow-up. Individual NPI hallucination scores include improvement, no change and worsening. This open longitudinal phase reuses the 2017 crossover cohort and has no dried fig exposure.

The original characterizes a sporadic Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease subtype in six patients using clinical, molecular and neuropathologic findings. The diagnostic cohort supplies no Parkinson exposure or visual hallucination count following dried fig intake.

The study compares functional MRI connectivity in 99 cases and 99 controls, focusing on connector hubs and motor or cognitive associations. It does not measure dried fig consumption or visual episode frequency.

The report relates genetic multiplication, clinical disease features and alpha-synuclein seeding or imaging in a family. The source addresses phenotype and neuropathology without measuring dried fig ingestion or a resulting episode-frequency outcome.

The review considers neuropathological explanations for incident dementia after depression. Hallucination history enters the differential diagnosis. It provides no culinary dried fig intervention or an outcome comparing visual episodes after eating.

The original describes a genetically defined parkinsonism phenotype and response to deep brain stimulation. Visual hallucinations are described among possible syndrome features. No dried fig exposure or food-timed episode count is recorded.

The review synthesizes functional and structural connectivity measures across dementia with Lewy bodies studies. It discusses visual hallucinations as a clinical correlate. It reports no fig intervention or clinical episode response to food intake.

Digital histology quantifies grey and white matter tau burden across different tauopathies. Clinical overlap and visual symptoms are context for diagnostic interpretation rather than a measured dried fig exposure or Parkinson visual episode follow-up.

The model predicts cognitive trajectories using clinical and biomarker data. The manuscript discusses visual hallucinations as a possible clinical correlate without a prospective fig intake comparison or food-timed count.

The review addresses microbial, immune and metabolic correlates across Lewy body diseases. Discussion of food or microbiome does not report a dried fig comparison paired with visual hallucination frequency.

Serial PET imaging evaluates regional cortical acetylcholinesterase-related change over follow-up. These physiological measures do not test dried figs or report a visual episode response to ingestion.

Two original cases report complex hallucinations around donepezil exposure. One describes cessation after withdrawal, and the other recurrence after re-exposure. These are medication time courses in dementia with no dried fig contrast or Parkinson visual episode assessment.

The review follows clinical evidence for intermittent treatment of off episodes and separates motor responses from adverse effects. The injected exposure and outcomes do not supply evidence about eating dried figs and Parkinson visual episode frequency.
